nodes.title: Yazma: Köşe yazısı
nodes.description: Üslup, bağlantı ve ikna araçlarıyla bir köşe yazısı yaz

exercises.prompt: Kültür, sanat ya da şehir hayatıyla ilgili seni rahatsız eden bir alışkanlık hakkında 260–300 kelimelik bir köşe yazısı yaz. Kişisel bir gözlemle başla, görüşünü iki gerekçeyle savun, karşı görüşü kabul edip yanıtla ve ikna araçlarıyla (retorik soru, Far from…, Surely…) akılda kalan bir sonla bitir.
exercises.model:
Save the Standing Ovation

Last Saturday, I watched a perfectly ordinary production of a well-known comedy. The jokes were fine, the actors remembered their lines, and nobody fell off the stage. When the curtain came down, the entire audience rose to its feet as if it had just seen the performance of the century.

This happens almost every night now, and I think it is time we talked about it. A standing ovation used to be a rare and special event. Today, in many theatres, it is simply the way an evening ends.

Why does this matter? Firstly, because praise that is given to everything means nothing. If a decent show and a truly extraordinary one receive the same reaction, the actors have no way of knowing the difference.

Secondly, the habit puts pressure on the audience. Many people stand not because they were moved but because everyone in front of them is standing and they cannot see the stage. Far from being a free choice, the ovation has become a social obligation.

Admittedly, there is a generous side to all this. People who have paid a great deal for their tickets want to feel that the evening was worth it, and standing up is one way of saying thank you. I have no wish to tell anyone how to enjoy themselves.

But gratitude and admiration are not the same thing. Warm, long applause from our seats is a perfectly good way to thank a cast. Let's save the standing ovation for the nights when we simply cannot stay seated, the nights we will still be talking about in ten years.

Surely those nights deserve a reaction of their own.
checklist: Yazıya kişisel bir gözlemle başladın
Görüşünü açıkça belirtip iki gerekçe verdin (Firstly…, Secondly…)
Karşı görüşü kabul edip yanıtladın (Admittedly…, But…)
En az üç ikna aracı kullandın (retorik soru, Far from…, Let's…, Surely…)
Görüşünü vurgulayan kısa ve akılda kalan bir sonla bitirdin

exercises.passage:
Subject: Your proposal for late opening

Dear Ms Okafor,

Thank you for your detailed proposal to keep the Central Library open until 10 pm on weekdays. It is clear that a great deal of thought has gone into it, and your members' enthusiasm is genuinely appreciated.

I am afraid, however, that we are not in a position to accept it in its current form. Visitor numbers after 7 pm have fallen slightly over the past two years, from an average of around 120 people an evening to just under 100. Extending opening hours across the whole week would therefore be difficult to justify, particularly as it would require two additional members of staff.

That said, I do not think this needs to be the end of the conversation. Visits on Thursday evenings, unlike the rest of the week, rose sharply last year, largely thanks to the language café that your group runs. We would therefore like to suggest a six-month trial in which the library stays open until 10 pm on Thursdays only. If numbers remain strong, we would be happy to look at a second evening.

I realise this is less than you had hoped for, and I would be glad to meet to discuss it. Perhaps you could let me know which days would suit you next week.

Yours sincerely,
Tomás Ferreira
Library Services Manager

exercises.passage:
The Visitors' Book

My grandmother kept a visitors' book by the front door, and every guest, however briefly they stayed, was expected to sign it. As a child I found this terribly old-fashioned. Who signs a book to say they came for tea?

It wasn't until after she died that I sat down and read it properly. The early pages were crowded: neighbours, cousins, old friends from work, people whose names meant nothing to me. Some had written whole paragraphs about the weather or the cake. Then, year by year, the entries grew shorter and further apart. In the last two years there were only three names, and two of them were mine.

I had always thought of myself as a dutiful grandson. I visited, after all. I brought flowers. But reading those pages, I saw what she must have seen each time she opened the book: the dates. Weeks, and then months, between one visit and the next.

On the final page, under my last signature, she had written a single line in her small, careful hand: "Came for tea. Stayed for an hour. Lovely."

I keep the book on my own shelf now. I have not yet been able to bring myself to sign it.
